name: Hassan Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for doing this, Hassan. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Can you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a production drill at an underground gold mine, a longhole rig, which drills fans of long holes up into the rock so the charge-up crew can load explosives and blast a whole stope, that's a big open chamber of ore. Most shifts I'm on level fourteen setting up the rig on the marks the surveyors painted, then drilling for eight hours, checking the angles, swapping rods. Lately I've been on a trial where for part of the shift I run the rig tele-remote from a booth near the shaft, with a joystick and four screens. I like that, honestly, I like anything new, but what wears me out is the stop-start, waiting two hours for a fitter because a hose blew.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my cousin Kwame on Station Road, he's doing an apprenticeship as an electrician. I'm single, no kids, and I'm good with money, I've got more than a year's expenses in index funds. I use AI every day, for everything, I had it explain the hydraulic manual for the new rig, I had it help me build a spreadsheet that logs my metres drilled per shift. I'm also in the union, my dad was a shop steward at a bus depot and he'd haunt me if I wasn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, honestly, a bit of a shame, I was hoping it'd do more. At work the boys would rib me, because I'm the one always showing them some AI trick on my phone in the crib room, that's our lunch room underground. Online I'd probably post something like, still useful, just not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it'd mean things stay comfortable. The tele-remote drilling would still spread because that's about safety and cost, not AI. I'd still be useful because I'm one of the few on my crew who actually likes the remote booth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI tools for the small stuff, manuals, planning, writing emails to the shift boss. I'd put my hand up for the next tele-remote trial on the jumbo, that's the development drill. And I'd keep putting a third of my pay into index funds, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly let down, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be a bit let down. What were you hoping for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it'd take the boring and dangerous parts off us and we'd all get shorter weeks for the same pay. My dad fought for a forty-hour week at the bus depot. I thought AI might get me a thirty-hour one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do your crewmates see the tele-remote booth the way you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. Big Tony calls it the gaming chair and says it's for people who don't like getting dirty. But Tony also doesn't have a smartphone, so I take it with a pinch of salt.

S0.say: He'd say it's a bit of a shame, he hoped AI would do more, and laugh it off with crewmates who rib him about his phone tricks. Online he'd post that it's still useful, just not magic.
S0.think: He thinks things stay comfortable for him, since tele-remote drilling spreads anyway for safety and cost reasons. He'd stay useful as one of the few who likes the remote booth.
S0.do: Keeps using AI for manuals, planning and emails, and volunteers for the next tele-remote trial on the development jumbo. Keeps putting a third of his pay into index funds.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly let down that AI didn't do more.
S0.quote: My dad fought for a forty-hour week at the bus depot. I thought AI might get me a thirty-hour one.
S0.fieldNote: Hassan is the rare miner who's disappointed by the plateau; he hoped AI would win shorter weeks, the way his father's generation won the forty-hour week. His progressive views and his love of new tech sit together easily. He sees the remote booth as a step up, not a threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say, this is good if we make sure it's shared, and I'd be arguing at union meetings for the training budget to be written into the agreement. With friends I'd be the optimist. Online I'd be posting about how the productivity gains should go into wages and shorter shifts, not just dividends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'm in a good spot. The guys who'll get hurt are the ones who won't touch the booth. I'm already in it, so I'm likely one of the people they keep, running three rigs from the surface instead of one underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company to put me through the automation technician course at the tech college, it's eighteen months part-time, and I'd pay for it myself if they wouldn't. I'd go for a full-time job in the remote operations centre the first time one comes up. And I'd help run sessions in the crib room showing the older guys the booth, because I don't want this to be a me-first thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited, and a bit guilty about the guys who'll struggle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilty. Who in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tony, actually, even though he gives me grief. He's forty-nine and he's the best hand driller on the site, he can tell from the sound of the rod if the ground is bad. A robot isn't going to hear what Tony hears, but the company will decide it doesn't need to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave the crew to go up to the remote centre?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I would. It'd sting a bit, leaving the crib room. But the pay's about the same, it's daylight, and my lungs would thank me in thirty years.

S1.say: He'd say this is good if the gains are shared and argue at union meetings for a training budget in the agreement. Online he'd post that productivity gains should go into wages and shorter shifts, not just dividends.
S1.think: He thinks he's in a good spot because he already likes the remote booth and is likely to be kept, running three rigs from the surface. The people hurt will be those who won't use it.
S1.do: Asks the company to fund an eighteen-month part-time automation technician course, paying himself if they refuse, and applies for the first full-time remote operations job. Runs crib-room sessions showing older crewmates the booth.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with some guilt about crewmates who will struggle.
S1.quote: A robot isn't going to hear what Tony hears, but the company will decide it doesn't need to.
S1.fieldNote: He frames his own advantage with real guilt, especially about Big Tony, whose skill he thinks the company will undervalue. He'd leave the crew for the remote centre without much hesitation. His union instincts show up as teaching others, not just bargaining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be saying this is the moment for something like a universal basic income, a regular payment to everyone, paid for by taxing the companies that own the AI. At work I'd be telling people to join the union now if they're not in it. Online I'd be a lot louder than I usually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it shakes me more than I'd admit. My whole plan was to be the guy who runs the robots, but if the AI can run the robots too, then the remote centre is just an AI in a server room. I've got savings, I'm young, I'd be fine for a year or two, but I don't know what the job after that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still do the automation course, but faster, full-time if I have to, in the first six months. I'd keep a bigger chunk of savings in cash instead of all in index funds. And I'd go hard with the union and with whatever party is pushing a basic income, door-knocking if it came to that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The kind where you keep checking your phone for news.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What does that short warning change for you, compared with your plans in the steadier picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It kills the ladder. In the steady one I go drill, then booth, then remote centre, then maybe technician. With two years, the ladder's still there but someone's sawing through the rungs while I'm climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that's still excited?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, honestly. If it really can do everything, maybe nobody has to go eight hundred metres down again. I just want to be sure that's a win for us and not just for the shareholders.

S2.say: He'd call for a universal basic income, a regular payment to everyone funded by taxing AI-owning companies, and tell coworkers to join the union now. Online he'd be much louder than usual.
S2.think: It shakes him more than he'd admit, because his plan to run the robots fails if AI runs them too. He'd be fine for a year or two on savings but doesn't know what job comes after.
S2.do: Rushes the automation course, full-time if needed, in the first six months and moves part of his savings from index funds into cash. Campaigns hard with the union and for any party backing a basic income.
S2.feel: Anxious, constantly checking the news, though still partly excited that nobody might have to go underground again.
S2.quote: With two years, the ladder's still there but someone's sawing through the rungs while I'm climbing.
S2.fieldNote: Fast AGI is the one picture that breaks his plan: his career ladder relies on humans supervising machines. Even so, he keeps a thread of hope that nobody would have to work underground. His politics move from 'share the gains' to a full basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same things about sharing the gains and a basic income, just calmer. At work I'd be running more of those crib-room sessions, and pushing the union to get a 'just transition' fund, money set aside to help workers move into new jobs, signed by 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can still climb at least a couple of rungs. I'd likely get into the remote centre, get the technician ticket, and earn well for a few years. After 2031, I'm thirty-two and I'll need something else, but I'd have time to see what that is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Do the automation course part-time, starting next intake, and apply for the remote centre in year one or two. I'd put a bit of money into a small side thing, maybe helping local businesses set up AI tools, because I already do it for free for my uncle's shop. Keep most savings in index funds, but more in cash than now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a buzzing way more than a scared way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned helping your uncle's shop. Tell me about that.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He runs a phone repair shop off Market Street. I set him up with an AI that answers customer messages and does his stock orders. It took me one Sunday and saved him six hours a week. That's the kind of thing I'd charge for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does five years change compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I can have a ticket in my hand and a bit of side money before it hits. Two years, I'm still sitting the exams when it lands. It's not the end point that's different, it's whether I'm ready when I get there.

S3.say: He'd repeat his calls for shared gains and a basic income, more calmly, and push the union for a just transition fund, money set aside to move workers into new jobs, signed by 2028.
S3.think: He thinks five years lets him climb a couple of rungs: the remote centre, a technician ticket and a few years of good pay. After 2031, at thirty-two, he'd need something else but would have time to see what.
S3.do: Starts the automation course part-time at the next intake and applies for the remote centre within a year or two. Starts a small side business setting up AI tools for local businesses and keeps more savings in cash.
S3.feel: Uneasy, but buzzing more than scared.
S3.quote: It took me one Sunday and saved him six hours a week. That's the kind of thing I'd charge for.
S3.fieldNote: With five years his entrepreneurial streak appears; the uncle's phone shop is a ready-made first customer. He explains clearly that the timing matters because of whether he'll have a qualification in hand. He keeps his progressive framing throughout, pushing for a transition fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if we start now, and I'd be pretty positive about it in public. At the union I'd push for a long-term deal where the company funds retraining every year for the whole decade. Online I'd post about what a four-day week could look like by 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think ten years is great for someone like me. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands, with a decade of experience in automation, maybe running my own small business by then. I'd worry more about the town than about myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, start the automation course and get into the remote centre. By year three or four, build up the AI setup business on the side, maybe go part-time at the mine. Keep investing most of my savings, and push the union to bargain for a shorter week as the machines take over more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and a bit excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing in the last couple of years before it lands?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Making sure I'm not only selling things AGI can do itself. Setting up AI for a shop is a job that disappears once AI can set itself up. Ten years is long enough that I'd be stupid to build my whole future on being the guy who understands the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the town you mentioned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's what keeps me up. Station Road has three pubs, two takeaways and a gym, and all of them run on mine wages. I'd want some of my union work to be about keeping the town alive when the pay packets stop.

S4.say: He'd be positive in public, saying ten years is plenty if work starts now. He'd push the union for a decade-long company-funded retraining deal and post online about a four-day week by 2030.
S4.think: He thinks ten years is great for someone like him, landing at thirty-seven with a decade of automation experience and maybe his own business. He'd worry more about the town than himself.
S4.do: Starts the automation course and moves to the remote centre in the first year, builds the AI setup business by year three or four and may go part-time at the mine. Keeps investing most savings and pushes the union to bargain for a shorter week.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough that I'd be stupid to build my whole future on being the guy who understands the robots.
S4.fieldNote: Hassan is the one person who looks ahead to his own plan becoming obsolete: he warns himself not to depend on 'understanding the robots'. His worry moves from himself to Station Road's businesses. The longer the warning, the more his concerns shift from his career to the community.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm usually the guy who's ahead of the change, and that's the only one where I'm not. What would help is a basic income that's actually decent, so people can retrain without panicking, and free courses at the tech college with no waiting list. I'm not scared of the machines. I'm scared of a world where only the people who own them get the day off.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what we'd do with the time. Everyone asks about losing work, nobody asks what you'd do with a free Tuesday. I'd fish, honestly, and help Kwame with his football team.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the machines. I'm scared of a world where only the people who own them get the day off.
portrait: Hassan is a 27-year-old production drill operator at an underground gold mine who shares a flat with his cousin and has over a year's expenses in index funds. He uses AI every day and is already on a tele-remote drilling trial, so he sees the remote operations centre as his next step. A union man like his father, he wants the gains of automation shared through shorter weeks or a basic income. The only picture that shakes him is AGI in two years, which would cut away his career ladder; with five or ten years he plans an automation qualification and a side business setting up AI for local shops.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, the only picture where he wouldn't be ahead of the change.
whatWouldHelp: A decent basic income so people can retrain without panic, and free tech college courses with no waiting list.
